Mozart's last three symphonies. These three works—Symphony No. 39 in E-flat major, No. 40 in G minor, and No. 41 in C major—represent the absolute peak of the Classical symphony. Composed in rapid succession in less than three months during the summer of 1788, they display a dramatic range and structural complexity that transformed the symphonic genre. Remarkably, there is no historical record of whether Mozart ever heard these symphonies performed, as he composed them during a period of financial hardship when his subscription concerts were failing.

The summer of 1788 saw Mozart complete Symphony No. 39 on June 26, No. 40 on July 25, and No. 41 on August 10—a remarkable feat of rapid composition. Symphony No. 41 in C major is universally known by its nickname Jupiter, likely coined by the publisher Johann Baptist Cramer to evoke the symphony's grand, godlike proportions. The most celebrated moment in the Jupiter comes in its fourth movement, which features a five-voice coda that stands as one of the greatest contrapuntal achievements in music history, combining five separate melodic themes simultaneously in double counterpoint.

Symphony No. 40 in G minor is one of only two minor-key symphonies Mozart wrote, often referred to as the "Great G minor" to distinguish it from No. 25. Its restless, driving opening theme in the violins is one of the most famous in the classical repertoire. Symphony No. 39 in E-flat major opens with a grand, slow introduction and is notable for completely omitting oboes, replacing their voice with clarinets instead. These three symphonies represent the culmination of Mozart's symphonic output, and they so impressed Beethoven that he heavily studied Symphony No. 40, copying out portions of its finale into his own sketchbooks while composing his Fifth Symphony.
